newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Prods Outlook - Gasoline production seen key.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Prods Outlook - Gasoline production seen key.

text.p: U.S. spot refined products traders should closely eye gasoline production across the country this week as the widely awaited peak summer demand season inches closer.

Traders said they expect activity in the Gulf Coast gasoline market to remain brisk this week amid talk some players were seeking to shore up gasoline supplies ahead of what is projected to be a record-demand season.

Gasoline stocks, just shy of 200 million barrels in the American Petroleum Institute's (API) latest inventory report, sat nearly 2.0 million barrels below the year-ago levels, though that deficit has shrunk steadily in recent weeks.

But traders are keeping close watch on when Tosco will restart its Trainer, Pennsylvania refinery. The refinery, closed by BP in January of 1996 before its sale to Tosco, is expected to return to service sometime after mid-May.
News that Tosco had purchased a Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) of West African crude for delivery at the beginning of May stoked speculation that the refinery could return earlier than thought.
However, the company was also seen covering short May-June gasoline crack spreads, which some took to indicate the refinery would not be producing product until at least June.

Reports late Friday Tosco would shut a crude unit at its Bayway, New Jersey refinery were denied by a source at the company Monday. He said work on a crude unit heater this week would not affect output at the 250,000 barrel per day unit.
New York Harbor traders will also closely eye the movement in the premium-grade gasolines, after the sharp jump in 93-octane reformulated D2 gasoline differentials last week.
Prompt D2 reached 8.00 cents over the May NYMEX print Friday, 4.00 cents up from its early week level, helped by reports of an outage at Star Enterprise's Delaware City refinery.
But a New Jersey environmental official on Monday said there appeared to be no trouble with a reformer at the refinery, though a steam unit there was down for maintenance.

New York Harbor No. 2 heating oil differentials were expected to remain firm during the early part of the week, helped by weather forecasts for colder-than-normal temperatures across much of the Northeast.
But that cold weather may be too little too late, traders said, since there appeared to be no real tightness in supplies.

"We've got a pretty high level of stocks right now," one trader said, adding that should limit the price impact. East Coast stocks of heating oil sat at 17.9 million barrels, about 3.4 million barrels above the year-ago level.
West Coast products were expected to continue last week's lackluster performance, which saw wholesale unleaded gasoline down two cents a gallon over the five days.

Fundamentals in the region were turning bearish, with refinery use up by 0.3 percentage points to 91.3 percent of capacity for the week ended April 11, as refiners churned out more gasoline ahead of heavier summertime demand.
"I don't think the market's going to take off. There's just too much gas," one West Coast trader said.
With little support, West Coast wholesale prices would be left tracking NYMEX products.
"I would say flat or maybe up a half cent if the Merc stays up," the trader said.
